lead: In a simply supported beam the tendon can be placed anywhere and the supports never notice: the beam is free to camber. A continuous beam is not free. Its intermediate supports stop the camber, so the prestress itself pushes and pulls on the supports and sets up extra secondary moments. Then the line of the concrete compression, the pressure line, no longer follows the tendon. A concordant cable is a profile that causes no secondary moments, and linear transformation is the rule that lets the designer move a tendon over the intermediate supports without moving the pressure line.
prereq: You need the pressure line and equivalent loads and the analysis of a propped or continuous beam by compatibility (deflection of a removed support set back to zero).

blocks.text: Take the prestress P with eccentricity e(x) below the centroid. The primary moment is P·e(x): the moment the tendon would cause if the beam were free. In a statically determinate beam it is the whole story, so every cable in a simply supported beam is concordant.

In a continuous beam the primary moment tries to bend the beam into a curve the supports do not allow. The supports react with secondary reactions, a set of forces that are in equilibrium on their own, and these cause secondary moments Ms. Because the reactions act only at supports, Ms is linear between supports. The resultant moment is the sum, and the pressure line sits at

blocks.where: e<sub>p</sub> is the eccentricity of the resultant concrete compression below the centroid in mm (negative means above); e is the tendon eccentricity; M<sub>s</sub> is the secondary moment, sagging positive, in N·mm; P in N. The fibre stresses due to prestress are P/A ± P e<sub>p</sub>/Z.

blocks.text: A cable is concordant when Ms = 0 everywhere, so the pressure line coincides with the tendon. A useful test: any profile drawn to the shape of the bending moment diagram of some real load on the continuous beam, at any scale, is concordant.

Move the tendon at the intermediate supports up or down, keep its eccentricity at the two end supports, and keep its shape (curvature) inside every span. Within each span the change is a straight line, so the profile has been changed by a linear transformation.

A straight-line change has no curvature, so the equivalent load of the tendon inside each span is unchanged. The only new loads are the kink forces exactly over the intermediate supports, which go straight into the supports without bending the beam. The resultant moment, and therefore the pressure line, is unchanged: whatever the transformation adds to the primary moment it takes away again as secondary moment. This is the theorem of linear transformation, usually credited to Guyon.

Two practical results follow. A linearly transformed concordant cable is still concordant only if the transformation is zero; any other transformation makes it non-concordant, with the same pressure line. And a non-concordant cable can always be transformed into the concordant one that runs along its own pressure line, which is what the worked example does. The designer is therefore free to choose the tendon position over the supports for cover, duct space and friction, while the concrete stresses stay those of the pressure line.

sections.h3: Two-span beam with a straight tendon

blocks.text: A straight tendon at constant eccentricity e in a two-span beam is the standard exam case, and it is not concordant. Freed from the middle support, the beam would camber up uniformly under the constant moment P e. Compatibility at the middle support (upward camber of the 2L beam, M<sub>0</sub>(2L)²/8EI, equal to the deflection of a central force R, R(2L)³/48EI) gives R = 3Pe/L downward there and 1.5Pe/L upward at each end. The secondary moment at the middle support is 1.5Pe, so the resultant there is 0.5Pe of the opposite sense: the pressure line rises from e below the centroid at the ends to e/2 above it at the middle support.

examples.question: A two-span continuous beam, each span 10 m, of section 300 mm × 600 mm, has a straight tendon with P = 1000 kN at 100 mm below the centroid over its full length. (a) Find the secondary reactions and the secondary and resultant moments at the middle support. (b) Locate the pressure line. (c) Find the concrete stresses due to prestress at the middle support. (d) Find a concordant cable by linear transformation and show that the stresses do not change.
steps: Primary moment M<sub>0</sub> = P e = 1000 × 0.1 = 100 kN·m along the whole beam, cambering it up.
(a) Compatibility: R = 3M<sub>0</sub>/L = 3 × 100/10 = 30 kN downward at the middle support; 15 kN upward at each end (they balance, as secondary reactions must).
Secondary moment at the middle support = 15 × 10 = 150 kN·m (sagging). Resultant = 150 − 100 = 50 kN·m sagging.

(b) e<sub>p</sub> = e − M<sub>s</sub>/P: at the ends 100 − 0 = 100 mm below; at the middle support 100 − 150 × 10⁶/(1000 × 10³) = 100 − 150 = −50 mm, that is 50 mm above the centroid; linear in between, e<sub>p</sub> = 100 − 15x mm with x in m from an end.
(d) Transform the tendon linearly: keep 100 mm below at the ends and raise it by 150 mm at the middle support, so e(x) = 100 − 15x mm in each span. It now lies on the pressure line.

Check: its primary moment at the middle support is 1000 × (−0.05) = −50 kN·m, that is −50 kN·m sagging, equal to the old resultant, so M<sub>s</sub> = 0: the new cable is concordant. The kink of 2 × 0.015 rad over the support pushes 1000 × 0.03 = 30 kN straight into the support.
Stresses at the middle support with the new cable: P/A ± P × 50/Z = 8.333 and 2.778 N/mm², the same as in (c).
examples.answer: The straight cable is not concordant: it causes 30 kN down at the middle support and 15 kN up at each end, a secondary moment of 150 kN·m and a resultant of 50 kN·m at the middle support, so the pressure line runs from 100 mm below at the ends to 50 mm above at the middle. Moving the tendon there gives a concordant cable with the same stresses, 8.33 and 2.78 N/mm².

traps: Saying a straight tendon with constant eccentricity is concordant in a continuous beam. It is not: it causes secondary reactions and moments (it is concordant only if e = 0).
Saying linear transformation leaves the reactions unchanged. It leaves the pressure line and the resultant moment unchanged; the secondary moments change.
Applying the transformation as one straight line over the whole beam and moving the end eccentricities. The ends stay fixed; the change is linear within each span.
Putting the secondary moment in as a curve. Secondary reactions act only at supports, so M<sub>s</sub> is straight between supports.
Using e instead of e<sub>p</sub> for the stresses in a continuous beam. The concrete sees the pressure line.

quiz.a: A tendon profile in a statically indeterminate structure that causes no secondary moments, so the pressure line coincides with the cable.

quiz.q: State the theorem of linear transformation.
quiz.a: If a cable in a continuous beam is moved at the intermediate supports without changing its end eccentricities or its shape within each span, the pressure line (resultant moment) does not change.

quiz.q: Why does every cable in a simply supported beam count as concordant?
quiz.a: The beam is statically determinate and free to camber, so prestress causes no reactions at the supports and no secondary moment.

quiz.q: Why is the secondary moment diagram linear between supports?
quiz.a: It is caused only by the secondary reactions, which are point forces at the supports; a beam loaded only at supports has a straight moment diagram between them.

quiz.q: Repeat the worked example with P = 1200 kN, e = 120 mm and spans of 12 m. Find R and the pressure line at the middle support.
Write the shape of a concordant cable for a two-span beam with equal spans L under uniform load.
quiz.a: Make e(x) proportional to that load's moment diagram: zero at the ends, hogging wL²/8 at the middle support (tendon above the centroid there) and a peak sagging 9wL²/128 at 3L/8 from each end (tendon below), so the eccentricities at the middle support and at 3L/8 are in the ratio 16 : 9.

quiz.q: The designer wants more cover over the middle support than the concordant cable allows. Explain how linear transformation helps and what it costs.
quiz.a: Lower the tendon over the support by any amount, keeping the ends and the span curvatures: the pressure line and the concrete stresses stay the same, so the stress checks still hold. The cost is a secondary moment and changed support reactions, which must be included in the ultimate design and the bearing loads.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern design the secondary moments are found by analysing the structure under the tendon's equivalent loads, and at the ultimate limit state they are added to the factored moments with a load factor of 1.0. Segmental and continuous box-girder bridges are designed this way. Search for secondary moments in continuous prestressed beams and the equivalent load method.

figure.caption: The straight tendon of the worked example in a two-span beam. The middle support holds the beam down with 30 kN, and the resulting secondary moment of 150 kN·m moves the pressure line from 100 mm below the centroid at the ends to 50 mm above it at the middle support; a tendon placed along that line is concordant.
